newsitem.title: CHINA: China exchange state debt trading hit by bank ban.
newsitem.headline: China exchange state debt trading hit by bank ban.

text.p: Trading on China's state debt spot and repurchase markets trading has been sharply hurt by Beijing's ban on state banks trading on the markets, analysts said on Friday.
Since the bank took effect three weeks ago, debt turnover on the Shanghai stock exchange, which handles 95 percent of China state debt trading, has fallen by more than 50 percent, they said.
"State banks used to account for around 80 percent of money supply on the Shanghai state debt repo market and 50 percent on the spot market," one state debt trader said.
"Their withdrawal is responsible for the sharp fall in the turnover in the past few weeks," he added.

The repo market was used by the banks as a reservoir of funds used to play the stock markets, and for a time last year, it was the biggest market in China in terms of trading volume due to the huge volatility on the stock markets.
Beijing banned the banks from trading in the markets from early June in order to help cool down the stock markets, analysts said.
"Despite the short-term negative impact on regional state debt trading, the ban serves to separate bank money from more risky funds in securities brokerages," a local banker said.

Since the ban, daily state debt repurchase trading turnover on the Shanghai bourse has fallen to around 2.5 billion yuan ($301.2 million) on average against more than five billion yuan in the first few months of this year, traders said.
Daily turnover for spot contracts has dropped about 50 percent to less than one million lots, traders said.

Interest rates for the repo contracts in Shanghai have also been fluctuating sharply and prices for spot state debt contracts have fallen steadily with the sharply lower fund supply making the contracts more vulnerable to changes, analysts said.

Securities houses and trust and investment companies have become the major traders on the debt markets, while the banks have been moving their liquidity and state debt trading operations to the national Chinese yuan interbank market based in Shanghai, analysts said.
"In the long run, interbank state debt trading can compensate for the loss on the regional markets," the banker said. "But rules governing the new way of trading is now lagging behind."
A total of 27 designated state banks are now trading state debt contracts on the interbank market, official media has reported.
Officials have been tight-lipped about trading on the interbank debt market, but sources indicate the volumes have been high, indicating large amounts of state debt trading have been shifted there.
